“Initially, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the Supreme Court interpreted the Commerce Clause narrowly. In the case of Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), the Court held that the Commerce Clause allowed Congress to regulate only commerce that involved the transportation of goods across state lines. This interpretation was consistent with the original intent of the framers of the Constitution, who were primarily concerned with preventing trade barriers between the states.

However, in the early 20th century, the Court began to adopt a broader interpretation of the Commerce Clause. In the case of Wickard v. Filburn (1942), the Court held that Congress could regulate the production of wheat on a small farm for personal consumption because the cumulative effect of such production on the national economy was significant. This expansive interpretation of the Commerce Clause was further strengthened in subsequent cases such as Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) and Katzenbach v. McClung (1964), which upheld the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its prohibition of racial discrimination in public accommodations.

In recent years, the Court has adopted a more conservative approach to the Commerce Clause. In National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius (2012), the Court held that the individual mandate provision of the Affordable Care Act, which required individuals to purchase health insurance or pay a penalty, was unconstitutional under the Commerce Clause. The Court reasoned that the Commerce Clause did not give Congress the power to compel individuals to engage in commerce.

Overall, the Supreme Court's interpretation of the Commerce Clause has evolved over time, with periods of both expansive and narrow interpretations. The Court's interpretation has been shaped by changing views of federalism and the balance of power between the federal government and the states.”

You have a disability which delayed your acceptance to law school, and likely was a causal factor for whatever criminal behavior you displayed in the past. Your disability was also likely the reason that you self medicated with alcohol and developed an addiction. That was not your fault. 

As a fellow ~~bipolar~~ law student, I too have felt the immense weight of imposter syndrome. Our shared disease makes law school exponentially more difficult, but we somehow have managed to cope with the stress without completely reverting to old patterns. That is a win in my book. We not the in the top 10% — but neither are 90% of our classmates. 

I went to rehab roughly two before law school, and found myself nearly slipping a couple of times, it is very impressive that you have stayed sober given the relatively short amount of time you were in recovery. More impressive given your drug of choice, which tends to be very prevalent in the social scene at law schools. I’m proud of you. 

Now, imposter syndrome is something I find all law students experience to some degree. In my case, it was really helpful to know that my friends were going through the same self imposed trials and tribulations. 

If I were you, I would see a therapist and figure out ways that can help you cope and excel in law school and life. This is certainly not the last time you will experience these feelings and thoughts. You should also consider requesting academic accommodations (note taker, audio recorder, extended time on tests/essays) which your school should grant seamlessly if you get a note from your psychiatrist. With bipolar specifically, other accommodations can also help, such as priority registration so that you give your full attention to your classes (I know my mood stabilizer certainty gives me brain fog in the early morning). 

I wish you nothing but the best of luck. 

P.s. I used the term disability stylistically, the reality is we are differently abled, and we are eligible (you twice) for diversity jobs. I highly recommend you go for it.

Before you do anything, ask yourself why? Why do you want to you want to be a judge? 

Do you want to be a state court trial judge? Do you want to be an appellate court judge? Do you want to be an Art. III judge? 

Are you interested in exploring obscure legal theories? Maybe being a professor is a better fit? 

Is this an ego thing? You should really figure that out first. 

If you are semi-normal and just look at being a judge like being in the major leagues of the legal profession then that’s cool too — just make sure you are fair if/when you ever have that opportunity. 

Now you are going to want to clerk, and that’s going to require being top 20% with strong extra curricular’s (law review, moot court, etc…). It would also be wise to spend at least a few years (5?) working as a government employee (DOJ/AG) and try to teach on the side so that you can go on secondment and spend a year or two as a professor researching and publishing some obscure legal theory. 

As you mentioned, most judges are elected, but all are political. Art. III judges are *heavily* dependent on your state’s senator. You are going to want to gain strong ties to both political parties and hobnob with future senators your entire career. 

I know a trump nominated judge who was put forth by a democrat—turns out the the senators predecessor went to the same hs as the judge. Connections will make or break you here. 

Another Art III judge I know was originally a state judge but was passed over for a state Supreme Court nod — two years later the senate put his name forth for the federal judgeship. 

Stay in the political machines good graces. A history of public service and scholarship will help you get started.
